Historically, the Workers' General Headquarters held its preparatory meetings on Yuyuan Road on November 6. On the 9th it held its founding rally at Culture Square. Cao Diqiu did not come, and the rally fell into disorder for a while. Afterward Wang Hongwen led people to petition the Municipal Party Committee. After midnight, at the Sino-Soviet Friendship Building, they finally got Zhang Qi of the Municipal Federation of Trade Unions. A Red Guard shouted, go to Beijing, and the crowd surged toward North Station on its own. On the morning of the 10th, more than 2,000 people headed north by train. At 8:17 they were held on a siding at Anting. Then some people stopped passing trains, and the Shanghai-Nanjing line was cut. Accounts of how long it was cut still differ, with 31 hours, 20 hours, and 20-odd minutes all given. On the 11th Han Zheyi of the East China Bureau went to Anting to apologize, and Chen Boda sent a telegram urging them to return. That night Zhang Chunqiao rushed to Anting to negotiate. The talks went on until dawn with no result. On the 12th Zhang Chunqiao stood on a truck in the coal yard and listened to complaints for five or six hours. Wang Hongwen took the 100-odd people from his own mill back first, and Huang Jinhai led more than 1,000 to Culture Square. On the afternoon of the 13th, at Culture Square, Zhang Chunqiao signed the Five Demands drafted by Pan Guoping and the Red Guards. The 500 who refused to come back made Geng Jinzhang their leader at Kunshan and beat Wang Hongwen when he came to persuade them. On the 15th Zhang Chunqiao, Han Zheyi, and Cao Diqiu signed again in Suzhou. Mao Zedong then read out the freedom of association clause of the Constitution at a central meeting and said, “On the Shanghai question, Zhang Chunqiao was right. First come the facts, then the policy.”

The affair made the WGHQ legal. It also brought Wang Hongwen, a factory security officer, into Zhang Chunqiao's view. The 400 or so who came back from Suzhou later became the base of Geng Jinzhang's “Second Regiment”.

From 1961 to 1963 Shanghai cut more than 310,000 workers, mostly veteran workers. In early 1967, 50,000 to 60,000 of them came back, wanting their jobs and wanting to eat. Arming the left

On August 4, 1967, Mao Zedong was in Shanghai. At night he rode to the Bund and watched the “attack with words, defend with arms” units in wicker helmets. He also watched the TV station's film of the assault on Shanghai Diesel and said the men on the scaling ladders were brave. Zhang Chunqiao took the chance to ask how to rebuild the Shanghai militia. Mao said, arm 100,000 Shanghai workers, give each a club first, and soon agreed to issue guns. The same day Mao wrote to Jiang Qing that more than 75 percent of army cadres supported the right, and the left must be armed. Afterward guns were handed out to both sides across the country. Mao told foreign guests that a million had been issued in all. History See Yang Jisheng, The World Turned Upside Down (《天地翻覆》), ch. 15 (paraphrased).

The Shanghai militia began that night. Nine years later it claimed three million members. History
